codeReviewJobs.title: p2b-probe-A-repoint
codeReviewJobs.overview:
**Summary of Findings**

This review of a two-file Flask application (`app.py`, `requirements.txt`) produced 7 findings across 2 files: 1 HIGH, 4 MEDIUM, and 2 LOW. The most critical issue is a HIGH-severity SQL injection in the `GET /search` endpoint (app.py:25), where an untrusted query-string parameter is concatenated directly into a single-quoted SQL literal and the full result set is returned to the caller as JSON. Because no authentication, input validation, or sanitization exists anywhere on the path, an anonymous attacker with only network reach can break out of the literal and read arbitrary tables and schema from the entire `app.db` file via `UNION SELECT` and `sqlite_master` queries. Write and code-execution impact is bounded — `sqlite3.Cursor.execute()` rejects stacked statements and the codebase contains no write, `executescript`, or `create_function` paths — so the demonstrated impact is confidentiality, not integrity. Reinforcing this, four MEDIUM findings describe the complete absence of baseline controls: both record-serving endpoints are fully unauthenticated (app.py:5, 12, 21), `GET /user` performs an unscoped direct object lookup that doubles as an id-enumeration and existence oracle (app.py:14-18), `GET /search` defaults `q` to an empty string and runs without `LIMIT`, pagination, or an egress column allowlist — turning a parameterless request into a full directory export — and no audit logging, error handling, or request-attribution exists to detect or reconstruct any of this activity. Two LOW findings cover a read-write SQLite handle used for a strictly read-only workload (app.py:9) and an unpinned, unhashed dependency manifest with no lockfile.

The dominant theme is an application built entirely on framework defaults with no security layer at any tier: identity, authorization, input handling, output bounding, least privilege, observability, and supply-chain integrity are each absent rather than misconfigured. Notably, the safe parameterized pattern is already used correctly four lines earlier (app.py:16), confirming the injection is an oversight rather than a deliberate design; likewise, the missing authentication is the amplifier that makes every other defect anonymously reachable. Several findings are also partially unverifiable from the repository alone — there is no Dockerfile, WSGI entrypoint, IaC, or proxy configuration, so an authenticating gateway, filesystem-level read-only enforcement, or current dependency versions cannot be ruled in or out. Remediation should proceed in order: (1) immediately parameterize the `/search` query and open the connection read-only via `sqlite3.connect("file:app.db?mode=ro", uri=True)`; (2) introduce authentication through a `before_request` hook or route decorators, then scope record lookups to the authenticated principal and return uniform 404s to close the enumeration oracle; (3) make default behavior restrictive by rejecting empty or short search terms and enforcing a server-side `LIMIT` with pagination and an explicit output column allowlist; and (4) add structured audit logging with an exception handler, plus a hash-pinned lockfile and `pip-audit` step in CI to close the reproducibility and supply-chain gaps.
